subtype: Stage 1: Work stress and quiet distance [Receiver]
passage: I'm Rajni, and I stayed with my sister Jasleen and her husband Harman for a week in Gurugram. Every evening was the same. Harman came in around nine, loosened his tie, said "hi" to both of us, and sat on the sofa with the TV on mute and his eyes half closed. He didn't seem angry, just emptied out. Jasleen would tell him something about her day, a funny thing her boss said, a plan for Sunday. He'd say "hmm" or "nice". By Thursday she had stopped telling. I found her in the kitchen, washing the same plate twice. "He doesn't need me here," she said. "I could be a lamp." I don't think Harman knew any of this. I'm not sure I did either, until then.

qa.q: What time did Harman usually come in?
What does Jasleen's remark "I could be a lamp" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals she feels invisible and unwanted, reading Harman's flat evenings as proof that her presence no longer matters.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this early stage?
qa.a: Jasleen could tell Harman how the quiet evenings feel to her, and Harman could explain he is drained, not uninterested, and offer a small time to connect.

qa.q: How does Harman seem to experience these evenings?
qa.a: He seems simply drained after work, not angry, and likely has no idea his quiet feels like rejection to Jasleen.

grounding: Shows a husband's exhausted, quiet evenings after work being read by his wife as a sign that she no longer matters.

subtype: Stage 1: Work stress and quiet distance [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: Arnab came home from the hospital IT desk at ten, ate standing up, and fell asleep with his phone on his chest. Gopika covered him with a sheet and told herself it was just a bad week.
Thursday: She'd made his favourite fish curry. He ate it, said "good", and went to sit on the balcony in the dark. She washed up alone, wondering when she had turned into furniture.
The next Tuesday: Gopika didn't cook. She didn't wait up either. When Arnab came in and asked, "Where's dinner?", she said, "Didn't think you'd notice." He looked confused, almost hurt. He had only wanted quiet. He hadn't known she was counting the empty evenings.

qa.q: What did Gopika make on Thursday?
qa.a: She made his favourite fish curry.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she washed up alone?
qa.a: She felt invisible, wondering when she had turned into furniture.

qa.q: What could each of them do at this stage to stop the distance growing?
qa.a: Gopika could say "I miss you in the evenings" before resentment sets in, and Arnab could name his tiredness and offer a small window of time.

qa.q: How does Arnab experience the "Didn't think you'd notice" reply?
qa.a: He is confused and almost hurt, because he only wanted quiet and never meant to reject her.

grounding: Shows a worn-out husband wanting only quiet and his wife reading the empty evenings as proof she no longer matters.
